title: From Justin to Kelly
full_review:
Some films seem like good ideas at the time, but the years prove unkind; other films are the cinematic equivalent of road kill off the bat. "From Justin to Kelly" (Fox), the pointless musical romantic comedy staring reality.TV's "American Idol" sweetheart Kelly Clarkson and frizzy.haired Justin Guarini, her fellow 15.minutes.of.famer, has skid marks all over it.

Despite leads who hitched their twin wagons to a star by singing on key, director Robert Iscove's lame ode to 1960s' beach party flicks hits a flat note on every level. Gone is the campy charm of teenybopper antecedents like "Where the Boys Are" and "Bikini Beach," replaced with a crass MTV.style thong.and.tequila fest, serving no other purpose than as a shameless cross.marketing vehicle to promote the show that spawned its two prodigiously.piped pop protagonists.

Make no mistake, while toning down the Dionysian debauchery of whipped.cream bikini contests and "margarita madness" parties to "PG" speed, the surf.and.song stinker promotes a casual carnality preoccupied with babes and booze.

To make a dumb story short, Clarkson and Guarini play star.crossed lovers on spring break in Fort Lauderdale, Fla. Clarkson .. as the Annette Funicello goody.two.shoes type .. is looking for sun and fun in the sand, carpooling it to Florida with fellow Lone Star lovelies Alexa (Katherine Bailess), the party girl, and brainy Kaya (Anika Noni Rose).

Guarini is the sensitive cog of a troika of beach party promoters, with their sights set on scoring more often than Michael Jordan. Accordingly, his "Pennsylvania Posse" consists of cardboard stereotypes, including ladies' man Brandon (Greg Siff) and computer geek Eddie (Brian Dietzen).

Predictably, Clarkson and Guarini's eyes and vocal cords meet across a crowded beach. However their romance is stymied by Alexa, jealous that Clarkson is getting all the attention; someone should tell her that anonymity in this film is a blessing.

The remainder of the unentertaining film is a silly pastiche of abysmal bubble.gum musical numbers including the aptly titled "I Won't Stand in Line" .. no one will for this clunker .. and tired narrative devices involving a tedious series of cell phone text.message miscues, as the lovelorn leads try to hook up. As if there was ever any doubt, they get what they deserve .. namely, each other .. and just in time to belt out a forgettable duet. About the only thing it rouses is the audience from its collective snoring.

The film's attempts at humor flounder, relying on hackneyed sunburn sight gags to elicit forced yuks. And while it is hard to dismiss their vocal talent, neither would have been cast in an infomercial, let alone a feature film, had it not been for the fortuitous turn of events on "American Idol." The cauliflower.domed Guarini is blessed with matinee looks made for radio, and Clarkson's acting elevates Funicello's frolicking to the level of "Antigone" by comparison.

There is a Tinseltown practice of attributing credit for movies with which the filmmaker refuses to associate his name .. usually because it is an undeniable bust .. to a fabricated scapegoat known among industry insiders as "Alan Smithee." Some viewers may applaud Robert Iscove for having the moxie to keep his name in the billing; others may more plausibly deduce that even the fictitious Mr. Smithee must draw the line somewhere.

One can only wonder, when the preordained sequel "From Clay to Ruben" opens, who will be wearing the bikini?

Due to sexually suggestive situations and frat.house humor, some mild language, as well as a glamorized attitude toward alcohol, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A.III .. adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG .. parental guidance suggested.
